verses.text: In Middle English manuscripts, you will sometimes find the word “the” abbreviated by a thorn letter (Þ) with a superscript e right above. In traditional printing, this would have been done not by printing a thorn and a superscript e on top each other, as that would have required one page to be set and printed twice; but by creating a special sort or type (a movable, metallic glyph used for early typesetting) that would have been treated as a ligature (like fi). This rare thorn glyph is only contained in a handful of digital fonts such as Noto Sans, Noto Serif, EB Garamond, or Inter, and is therefore difficult to display even in modern typography. When William Caxton in the 1470s imported his printing press from Cologne, Germany to Westminster, England, he faced a similar issue: the Germans did not supply him with a thorn type, thus forcing him to replace the thorn with a y. Hence, when “the King’s printer” Robert Barker printed the 1611 King James Version of the Bible, that new glyph, now with a y instead of a thorn, had already become a standard of Early Modern English typography. You will find it, for example, in Shakespeare's First Folio from 1623 or in some of John Milton’s handwriting. Modern Internet browsers render these letters by Combining Diacritical Marks, in this case U+0079 for the lowercase y and U+0364 for the superscript e, which is then passed on to a Text Shaping Engine (such as HarfBuzz for Google Chrome or CoreText for Apple devices) to convert the data into visible glyphs. Or in other words, the early printers did not stack these two glyphs, but our modern devices do. This tedious rendering process is done because there exists no Unicode for the yͤ glyph, though it allows for more than a handful of digital fonts to display this glyph, even though it is not contained in their set. Hence, when you see the yͤ glyph in the 1611 KJV, read it as “the”, not as “ye”. Such as in this case: “That which was from yͤ beginning...” = “That which was from the beginning...” The biblical text of the 1611 KJV holds a total of 187 instances where this abbreviation was used, such as here in 1 John 1:1, in 1 John 4:10, in Judith 1:1, etc. Like most abbreviation, the yͤ was used for line justification, to squeeze the line so it fits into the narrow columns of the 1611 KJV.
